lines.text: In 1999, engineers started digging the dirt out from under the Leaning Tower of Pisa, to stop it falling over.
You see, one wrong scoop, and fourteen thousand tonnes come down.
It starts sinking in 1178, on a foundation three meters deep in soft clay.
Then war stops the work for almost a century. The clay settles, and that saves it.
In 1934, Mussolini's engineers pump in cement. It lurches the wrong way.
By 1990, it leans five and a half degrees, and Italy shuts it.
So they stack six hundred tonnes of lead on the high side.
In 1995, they freeze the ground to swap the lead for anchors.
One September night, it lurches more than it had all year.
Pisa's mayor says "a plumber with a toilet jack" would've done better.
Locals pelt the engineers' cars with tomatoes.
So how do you save a falling tower by taking the ground away?
You see, the low side is so soft that one touch could topple it.
So they drill under the high side, pulling dirt out a bucket at a time.
It's like fixing your wobbly table by trimming the long leg.
Thirty-eight cubic meters later, the top has swung back forty-five centimeters.
Then they stop on purpose after half a degree, too little to notice.
Bookies took bets it wouldn't see this century. Now it's safe for at least two hundred years.
